sceneHappening: Timothy is sent back, returns with good news, and Paul prays for love and holiness until the Lord comes
summary: When Paul could not endure it any longer, he thought it good to be left behind alone at Athens, and sent Timothy, "our brother and God's servant in the Good News of Christ," to establish them and comfort them concerning their faith, that no one would be moved by these afflictions, for they themselves know that they are appointed to this. When Paul was with them, he told them beforehand that they would suffer affliction, "even as it happened, and you know." For this reason, when he could no longer endure it, he sent to know their faith, lest by any means the tempter had tempted them and their labor would be in vain. But now that Timothy has come from them to Paul and has brought good news of their faith and love, and that they have good memories of Paul, longing to see him as he longs to see them, Paul is comforted about them in all his distress and affliction through their faith; "for now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord." What thanks can Paul render to God for them, for all the joy with which he rejoices for their sake before God, as he prays "exceedingly night and day that we may see your face and may perfect that which is lacking in your faith"? He prays that God himself and the Lord Jesus may direct his way to them, and that the Lord may make them "increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we also do toward you; to the end he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints."
whySettingMatters: This chapter reveals the reason for the letter. Paul had been driven out of Thessalonica after only a few weeks, and he could not rest until he knew whether the church had survived the pressure. Timothy, the younger co-worker, was the one he trusted to go, and Paul's relief at the news is the emotional center of the letter: "now we live." The reference to being "left behind alone at Athens" is the only hint in Paul's own letters of how lonely that stop was (compare Acts 17:16-34). Paul says he told the church beforehand that they would suffer, and that this was part of the Christian path, an idea that runs through the letter and through the New Testament. "The tempter" is Satan, and Paul's fear was that persecution might have led them to give up. The prayer in 3:11-13 is the hinge of the letter: it sums up the first half (a prayer to see them) and looks ahead to the second half (love, holiness, and the coming of the Lord). "With all his saints" is debated: it may mean holy ones (believers) or angels who come with the Lord, as in 2 Thessalonians 1:7.

questions: Paul says he could not bear not knowing how they were doing. What does that reveal about how he related to churches?
He tells them suffering is something "we are appointed to." How does that change expectations about the Christian life?
"Now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord." What do you think Paul means?
His prayer asks that their love would "increase and abound." Why love, of all things, to pray for?
